title: Sorin and the Storm Sprite's Secret
markdown:
Gadzooks! In the grand country of the High Peaks, where mountains pierced the clouds like watchful giants, lived an elf named Sorin Swiftfoot. No grand city. Roots as steadfast as wind-battered firs. Eyes the colour of moss after spring rain, seeing everything: eagles’ arcs, wind in purple heather, the faintest tremor of a twig. Mountain-bred, brilliant as tumbling streams.

His closest companion, not yet quite claimed, was a small shy pine marten: fur the warm dappled brown of sun-drenched earth, a whirlwind of nervous energy behind rocks and ferns. The marten had chosen Sorin. Sorin called him Pudding, for the way he’d puff his chest when feeling a little bold. Pudding had a nose for trouble.

One crisp morning Old Man Thistlewick’s smoke was not the usual steady plume. A frantic sputtering puff. “That doesn’t look right,” Sorin murmured. Thistlewick, kind as a summer breeze, never sent such a signal unless something was truly amiss.

“Come on, Pudding.” Pudding perked, chirped, and was at Sorin’s boots, vibrating. Pudding had a nose for trouble.

They followed a winding path through alpine flowers that nodded as if they, too, had opinions about weather. The sky put on a show: a dark cloud shaped like a grumpy badger, then bruised purple. Wind roared like a frustrated giant, whipping Sorin’s hair, making tall firs groan. Pudding scrambled onto Sorin’s shoulder instead of hiding, nose twitching. Rain fell in fat theatrical drops that bounced like pebbles and sparkled. Lightning giggled in zigzags. Thunder chuckled. Pine shadows striped the path like a curtain yanked too fast.

“The sky has decided to put on a grand performance.” Pudding chirped urgently. Pudding had a nose for trouble.

Closer to the gorge, the peculiar distress multiplied. A washing line of Thistlewick’s neighbours had become a row of frantic flags. A goat stood on a roof as if that had been the plan all along. Mistress Honeycomb waved a flour-dusted apron. Berry bushes knocked over, harvest scattered. “It keeps swirling and stopping, like a dancer who’s forgotten her steps.” Mr Grainwright struggled with a flapping mill-sail, face grim. “As if something’s playing with the wind. Blows fiercely, changes course, stops dead when you need it most.”

Sorin looked at Pudding. Pattern. Intention. “Someone is making it behave this way.” A chance boast, light as heather: “If the sky wants an audience, we’ll give it a director. Three jobs, Pudding. Baker, miller, chimney. We’ll trick a storm into being useful.” Hyperbole, yes: seven squalls with one marten, if the boast held.

Pudding led not to Thistlewick’s cottage but up toward a jagged hidden peak, rock formations like petrified faces. The climb was scree and wet lichen; Sorin’s cloak became a sail he had not asked for. The storm grew more theatrical: a rainbow appeared and vanished as if a child had erased it, glittering confetti, a cinnamon gust, thunder like a drumroll. Pudding darted up a ledge Sorin would never have noticed, to a small shadowed opening that smelled of ozone and damp moss.

Inside, on a moss-covered stone, a Storm Sprite no bigger than Sorin’s hand, dragonfly wings, starlight eyes, tapping a shimmering crystal with a twig. Each tap intensified the flair — a boom for the gorge, a swirl for the mill, a sneeze of glitter for no reason at all. Sheepish guilt when it saw them. “I was just terribly bored. So quiet up here. I’ve been practicing. Then everyone got upset, and the chimney went funny, and the berries scattered.” Pudding hopped onto the stone as if he had been invited, which, in a way, he had: Pudding had a nose for trouble, and trouble had a cave.

“Three tasks, then,” Sorin said, as if an invisible king had imposed them, “and we’ll bluff the weather into behaving.”

Task one: Mistress Honeycomb’s berries. Sorin did not shout at the sky. He asked the sprite to tap for a wind that only righted fruit — a mischievous fix that looked like accident. Berries rolled home as if ashamed of the mud. The baker, seeing the harvest return, declared she had always known weather had manners, if you asked politely.

Task two: Mr Grainwright’s mill. Sorin had the sprite blow just enough, then stop, then blow, until the miller thought he had tamed a fussy wind himself. The sail filled with steady purpose. Mighty and simple, both fooled: miller proud, sprite delighted at being taken for a professional breeze.

Task three, the daring bluff: Old Man Thistlewick’s frantic smoke. Sorin told the sprite the chimney wanted a partner, not a rival. One gentle puff timed to a chuckle of thunder. The smoke rose perfect, and Thistlewick, who had been ready to appease mountain gods with honey cakes, decided the gods had merely sneezed. He put the cakes back in the tin, which was, Pudding thought, the truest magic of the afternoon.

Rivals turned: baker and miller stopped blaming each other, blamed “theatrical weather,” and then, seeing the berry-righting and the steady mill, blamed nobody. The sprite, who had thought volume was the only applause, learned a quieter encore. They sat together on the moss stone while the crystal learned to hum instead of shout. Pudding showed how a mist could settle like dew. Sorin showed how a rainbow could linger just long enough to be admired, not so long it blocked the road. The valley below, watched from the cave mouth, changed colour from bruise to gold.

“You’re not angry?” the sprite whispered.

“Not angry. Friendlier shows.” Pudding batted an iridescent feather. Together they taught soft rain for bushes, lingering rainbows, mists like dew. The crystal hummed. The valley cleared. Sun benevolent. Chimney comforted. Berries as if by magic. Mill steady.

Sorin and Pudding walked down a true team, picking their way past berry-stained mud that now looked almost intentional, like a recipe. Pudding trotted, chattering, tail flicking. The valley gold and serene. Mistress Honeycomb had already baked something that smelled of apology and jam. Mr Grainwright waved from the mill as if they had planned the wind together. Old Man Thistlewick’s chimney wrote a single calm sentence of smoke against the clearing sky. Sorin had meant only to help a neighbour and had, with a marten who puffed like pudding, tricked a storm into kindness.

And as for the Storm Sprite? On particularly starry evenings you might catch a tiny iridescent sparkle, a gentle reminder that the best performances bring shared joy. Wink, if you like: the badger-cloud never did learn the steps, but it stopped scowling, which is almost as good as seven storms with one twig.
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for older children
